l.corrientes.genero.descripcion: Since the late 1980s, Assyriology has been asking how cuneiform texts constructed the masculine, the feminine and what lay between the two. Inanna/Ishtar, goddess of sexuality and war who can "turn a man into a woman and a woman into a man", is the starting point. Studying her has brought to the fore the specialists of her cult (gala/kalû, assinnu, kurgarrû), who are now described as an institutionalized gender otherness rather than as "eunuchs" or "sacred male prostitutes". The relationship between Gilgamesh and Enkidu has also been read anew. This trend calls for caution: modern categories such as "homosexual" or "trans" should not simply be carried over into the past.
l.corrientes.ecocritica.descripcion: Ecocriticism reads the Mesopotamian myths as the first texts to tell of a conflicted relationship between the city and its environment. The felling of the Cedar Forest and the death of its guardian Humbaba are interpreted as a transgression, even as an ecocide, which the epic itself seems to regret. Atrahasis and the flood stories have been read in relation to overpopulation, salinization and climate change. The new fragments of Tablet V, which describe a forest teeming with life, have strengthened this approach.
l.corrientes.ideologia.descripcion: This approach treats the myths as instruments of power. The Enuma Elish legitimizes the supremacy of Marduk and, with it, that of Babylon. In Assyria there were versions in which Ashur takes Marduk's place, and the poem prompted "countertexts" and commentaries with political intent. Researchers also study how the Neo-Assyrian kings used reliefs, inscriptions and rituals (such as the Akitu) as propaganda, and how the Sumerian King List constructs a single, continuous kingship.
l.corrientes.mortalidad.descripcion: Psychological and existential readings make Gilgamesh the first great story about the fear of death, grief for a friend and maturity. The hero who loses the plant of youth ends up accepting his mortal condition and his work, the walls of Uruk. Some studies link this theme with gender and age: the Epic would tell how a young man reaches adulthood. The stories of Adapa and Etana, in which immortality is offered and lost, are also added to it.
l.corrientes.trauma.descripcion: The Sumerian laments for the destruction of Ur, of Sumer and Ur, of Nippur or of Uruk are read today as cultural responses to a collective catastrophe: the fall of the Third Dynasty of Ur around 2000 BC. In them the city goddess weeps for her ruined city, and they are often compared with the biblical Lamentations. Along similar lines, the poem of Erra and Ishum is interpreted as a reflection on the violence Babylon suffered in the 1st millennium. The explicit application of "trauma theory" to these texts is still recent and not very systematic.
l.corrientes.poscolonial.descripcion: This approach asks to whom Mesopotamia and its tablets belong. It examines how 19th-century European archaeology turned Assyria and Babylon into a prelude to the Bible and to "the West" and sidelined modern Iraq. It also analyzes the looting of the Iraq Museum in 2003, the plundering of sites, the illegal antiquities market (with the case of Hobby Lobby and the Gilgamesh Dream Tablet, returned in 2021) and the destruction of Nimrud and Nineveh by the Islamic State in 2015. Zainab Bahrani, among others, has argued that Iraq should be the protagonist of its own past.
l.corrientes.digital.descripcion: Mass digitization of tablets, open databases and artificial intelligence are changing the way texts are reconstructed. The Electronic Babylonian Library (eBL) project at LMU Munich joins thousands of fragments with matching algorithms. There are already neural models that produce a first draft translation from Akkadian into English. Thanks to these tools, new passages of Gilgamesh, unknown hymns and joins between fragments scattered across museums around the world are coming to light.
l.entradas.inanna-ishtar.lectura:
For gender studies, Inanna/Ishtar is the central figure of Mesopotamian mythology. Rivkah Harris (1991) presented her as "paradox and coincidence of opposites": she is feminine and a warrior, lover and destroyer, and she is neither wife nor mother. She is a goddess who breaks the boundaries that society drew. Her ability to alter the gender of her devotees, mentioned in several hymns, has made Ishtar a touchstone for queer readings.

Current criticism also tones down some ideas: the "sacred prostitution" associated with her cult is now seriously doubted for lack of solid evidence. Zainab Bahrani and other scholars have analyzed how Western scholars projected onto Ishtar their own fantasies about "Oriental" sexuality.
l.entradas.gilgamesh.lectura:
Gilgamesh is today the Mesopotamian text that receives the most readings. Gender studies debate whether the relationship with Enkidu is erotic. Susan Ackerman (2005) argues that the poem's language of love (Gilgamesh "embraces Enkidu like a wife" and mourns him like a bride) serves to mark the heroes as liminal figures; she does not read it as a "marriage" in the modern sense. Tzvi Abusch has studied the tension between the masculine and the feminine in the work and Gilgamesh's rejection of Ishtar.

Existential readings make the quest for immortality the first great story about grief and the acceptance of death. Ecocriticism rereads the felling of the Cedar Forest as a transgression against nature. The editions by Andrew George (2003) and Sophus Helle (2021) already incorporate fragments discovered after 2000.
l.entradas.enuma-elish.titulo_actual: A myth in the service of empire
l.entradas.enuma-elish.lectura:
Today the Enuma Elish is not read as a timeless "Babylonian Genesis" but as a political text. Its function is to explain why Marduk and his city, Babylon, head the pantheon and the world. It was recited at the Akitu festival. Eckart Frahm (2010) has studied how, between 900 BC and AD 500, the poem was revised, commented on and challenged. There was an Assyrian version with Ashur as protagonist, and texts such as Erra and Ishum or parts of the biblical Genesis would function as "countertexts".

Gender readings, for their part, note that the cosmic order is born from killing a primordial mother, Tiamat.
l.entradas.marduk.titulo_actual: The god as a political program
l.entradas.marduk.lectura: The figure of Marduk is studied as an example of how a local deity becomes the supreme god at the same time as his city rises. The exaltation of Marduk in the Enuma Elish, with his fifty names, is interpreted as a form of Babylonian political theology tending toward henotheism. The removals of his statue by the Assyrians, the Elamites and the Hittites are read as symbolic blows against Babylon.
l.entradas.ashur.lectura: Ashur, god and city at once, is used today to analyze Neo-Assyrian ideology. The king acted as his vicar, and military expansion was presented as a divine mandate. Among the most cited studies are the "Assyrianization" of the Enuma Elish, which puts Ashur in Marduk's place, and the propaganda of the palace reliefs. W. G. Lambert, however, warns that the change of names was an incomplete reworking and not a new edition of the poem.
l.entradas.tiamat.lectura: Feminist readings see in Tiamat's death at the hands of Marduk the passage from a primordial female principle to a male, urban order. Assyriology qualifies this: the text does not present Tiamat as a prehistoric "Mother Goddess" overthrown, which is a modern myth. Ecocriticism and pop culture have turned her into the symbol of watery chaos and of the ocean, and she appears as a monster or as a goddess in video games such as Smite or Fate/Grand Order.
l.entradas.descenso-inanna.titulo_actual: A journey of death and rebirth
l.entradas.descenso-inanna.lectura: The Descent of Inanna is one of the favorite texts of feminist spirituality and Jungian psychology. It is read as a journey of stripping away and rebirth: at each gate the goddess surrenders an insignia of power. Within Assyriology, gender readings study the rivalry between the two sisters, Inanna and Ereshkigal, and the role of the genderless beings (kurgarra and galatura) that Enki creates to rescue her. These beings are related to the specialists of Inanna's cult.
l.entradas.dumuzi-tammuz.lectura: The love songs between Inanna and Dumuzi are studied today as erotic poetry that celebrates female desire. They are no longer accepted uncritically as scripts for a supposed ritual "sacred marriage". Dumuzi's death and the lament for him are read as a cycle of collective mourning, related to the weeping for Tammuz recorded in the Bible (Ezekiel 8:14).
l.entradas.ereshkigal.lectura: Ereshkigal has been reread as Inanna's "shadow" in Jungian psychology. Gender studies are interested in her female sovereignty and her loneliness. The myth of Nergal and Ereshkigal is interpreted as a negotiation of power and desire within the divine couple. In pop culture (for example Fate/Grand Order) she has gone from a fearsome figure to a likable character.
l.entradas.nergal-ereshkigal.titulo_actu: Power and desire in the Underworld
l.entradas.nergal-ereshkigal.lectura: This myth is read today in terms of gender and power. In the late version, Ereshkigal demands Nergal as her husband and threatens to raise the dead if he is not sent to her. It is a rare example of female desire prevailing in the pantheon. Other readings see it as a story of how a god of war and plague is integrated into the world of the dead.
l.entradas.atrahasis.lectura: Anne D. Kilmer (1972) read Atrahasis as a myth about overpopulation. The "noise" of humans that keeps Enlil from sleeping would be their excessive numbers, and the poem ends with control mechanisms: infant mortality and priestesses who have no children. Current ecocriticism takes up this idea to talk about ecological limits, droughts and famines, which in the poem come before the flood. Political readings focus on the origin of labor: the lesser gods rebel against the burden of corvée work.
l.entradas.diluvio-ziusudra.titulo_actua: The flood in times of climate crisis
l.entradas.diluvio-ziusudra.lectura: In times of climate emergency, the Mesopotamian flood is read as the cultural memory of the catastrophic floods of the alluvial plain and as a warning about the fragility of civilization. The environmental humanities compare it with today's stories about rising sea levels. Irving Finkel, of the British Museum, presented the "Ark Tablet" in 2014, which describes a round ark (a kind of giant coracle). With it he revived public interest in the relationship between this story and that of Noah.
l.entradas.erra-ishum.titulo_actual: Violence and the trauma of Babylon
l.entradas.erra-ishum.lectura: Erra and Ishum is interpreted as a poetic reflection on indiscriminate violence and civil war. Babylon suffered that violence in the first centuries of the 1st millennium BC. Eckart Frahm also considers it a "countertext" to the Enuma Elish: while Marduk is absent from his throne, chaos breaks loose. Its use as an amulet against plague interests those who study how societies process catastrophe.
l.entradas.lista-reyes.lectura: The Sumerian King List is no longer considered a chronicle but an ideological construction. It presents a single kingship that "descends from heaven" and passes from city to city, when in reality many dynasties ruled at the same time. In this way it legitimized the kings of Isin and of other later dynasties. Its reigns of thousands of years before the flood, which proponents of the ancient astronaut theory read literally, are explained today as a symbolic chronology.
l.entradas.enki-ninhursag.lectura: Enki and Ninhursag is read today through the body and gender: a male god of fresh water impregnates generation after generation of goddesses, and the mother goddess steps in to punish him and then to heal him. Feminist readings debate whether the story depicts sexual violence or criticizes it. Environmental readings focus on the water that makes Dilmun fertile, a land that was once barren.
l.entradas.inanna-enki-me.titulo_actual: A goddess who carries off civilization
l.entradas.inanna-enki-me.lectura: The story of Inanna, who gets Enki drunk and carries off the me (the powers of civilization) from Eridu to Uruk, is read as a political myth. It would explain how Uruk became the religious center. It is also read as a story of female cunning. Among the me are offices of Inanna's cult with an ambiguous gender, which gender studies make use of.
l.entradas.lugal-e.lectura: In Lugal-e, the god Ninurta defeats the demon Asag and his army of stones, passes judgment on each stone and channels the waters toward the Tigris. The environmental humanities read it as a myth about how a landscape is made habitable: the control of mountains, minerals and irrigation. Political readings see Ninurta as a model of the warrior king.
l.entradas.enlil.titulo_actual: A god with myths still to be discovered
l.entradas.enlil.lectura: Enlil, the god who sends the flood because humans make too much noise, appears in ecocritical readings of Atrahasis and in gender readings of the myth of Enlil and Ninlil. The latter is discussed today as a story of sexual violence punished by the assembly of the gods. The publication in 2024 of tablet Ni 12501 by Jana Matuszak made known an unknown myth of Enlil. In it, the storm god Iškur, son of Enlil, is trapped in the Underworld and only the fox offers to rescue him.
l.entradas.tablilla-perdida-enlil.titulo: Ni 12501: a myth that took a century to be published
l.entradas.tablilla-perdida-enlil.lectur: Tablet Ni 12501 was excavated at Nippur in the 19th century and is kept in the Istanbul Archaeology Museums. Samuel Noah Kramer mentioned it in the 1950s as "another Enlil myth, still unpublished". Jana Matuszak edited it in full in the journal Iraq (vol. 86, 2024). It dates to the Early Dynastic IIIb period (around 2400 BC) and tells how Enlil gathers the gods to rescue Iškur from the Underworld. The tablet breaks off before the end. It is a good example of how many texts are still waiting in museum storerooms.
l.entradas.adapa.lectura: Adapa follows Enki's advice and refuses the "bread and water of life". Existential readings pair him with Gilgamesh: both stories explain why human beings, however wise, remain mortal. Adapa is also compared with the Adam of Genesis, although today it is ruled out that one derives directly from the other.
l.entradas.etana.titulo_actual: Infertility and a flight to heaven
l.entradas.etana.lectura: King Etana rises to heaven on the back of an eagle to obtain the "plant of birth". Current readings pay attention to a theme long little studied: infertility and the anxiety to have an heir who would secure the dynasty. In the story the intimate and the political intersect.
l.entradas.akitu.lectura: The Babylonian New Year festival is studied as a stage for power. In it, the king was humiliated and reinvested before Marduk, and the Enuma Elish was recited. Historians debate how much of that ceremony is a modern reconstruction. Scholars have also studied how the Assyrian kings, from Sennacherib on, moved the Akitu to Ashur to appropriate its prestige.
l.entradas.biblioteca-asurbanipal.titulo: From the royal library to the digital library
l.entradas.biblioteca-asurbanipal.lectur: The thousands of fragments from Nineveh held by the British Museum are the main material of the Electronic Babylonian Library, Enrique Jiménez's project at LMU Munich. Its Fragmentarium, opened to the public in February 2023, uses algorithms to join loose pieces. At the same time, the library is read as a project of power: Ashurbanipal gathered the knowledge of Babylon, often by force, in order to control it.
